title: Zuckerberg's Letter Shows Most Schools Are Getting AI Exactly Backwards
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Bauschard uses Mark Zuckerberg's August 10 letter 'The Future is for Everyone' as a lens to argue that most schools have inverted the correct response to abundant AI: rather than restricting student access to protect against misuse, schools should be distributing frontier AI as widely as possible, because concentrated access -- not AI itself -- is what reproduces inequality. He takes seriously Zuckerberg's central claim that 'there is no such thing as a singular benevolent superintelligence,' reasoning through what it means at classroom scale: a student with an unrestricted frontier model at home learns that ideas become things in an evening, while the student in the next desk whose school blocked the model learns that ideas are 'things you write down for a grade' -- and argues restriction policies don't protect students from wasting AI, they simply protect them from having it. The piece is sharply critical of school AI-blocking as institutional self-protection dressed as caution, while pointing to university oral-exam and live-building assessment shifts as evidence that the redesign work is already underway elsewhere. Bauschard closes with a concrete list of institutional changes -- universal frontier-model access, teachers as coaches, authorship-centered curriculum, and pressure on largely silent accreditors -- arguing the correction 'costs less than the compliance software many districts are buying.'
points: Reframes Zuckerberg's 'no singular benevolent superintelligence' argument at classroom scale: a student with unrestricted AI access learns that ideas become things in an evening, while a student at a school that blocks AI learns that ideas are 'things you write down for a grade.'

Argues restriction policies fail on their own terms: 'Restriction doesn't protect your students from wasting the tool. It protects them from having it,' reframing what looks like caution as reproduction of exactly the access-inequality the letter warns about.

Points to concrete evidence that redesign is already happening elsewhere -- Cornell's twenty-minute Socratic oral defenses, Penn's shift toward in-person assessment, an NYU Stern AI-driven oral exam -- as proof the response isn't hypothetical or radical, just uncommon in K-12.

Identifies accreditors' silence as 'the load-bearing failure' in the system, arguing individual schools that redesign around AI take on real institutional risk precisely because no standards body has updated what a 2026 school should be accountable for.
quotes: None of that lets educators off the hook. Because whatever you think of the messenger, the letter is a fairly accurate description of the world our students are walking into.
One student has a frontier model. The others don't. The letter tells you exactly who that student is.
Now look at the kid in your fourth-period class whose school blocked the model and whose family can't buy the subscription. Same age, same curiosity, no evening.
We did not eliminate the power asymmetry the letter warns about. We reproduced it inside the one institution built to interrupt it, and put an acceptable use policy on the door.
Restriction doesn't protect your students from wasting the tool. It protects them from having it.
The single largest expansion of access to individualized instruction in the history of formal education showed up, priced at zero or close to it, and the institutional response was to restrict it.
And the accreditors and standards bodies have been almost entirely silent. That's the load-bearing failure, because schools follow those signals.
